introduction: The guide begins with an image and a challenge. The Manifestations of God are artists whose pictures hang in human hearts; and a clergyman asks by what authority Bahá’u’lláh is placed with Abraham, Moses and Jesus. The readings answer by describing a station: a mirror in which an unknowable God is seen, a knowledge that is not acquired, a human life that is tested and a divine reality that is not, a voice that says “I am but a servant” and “all turn unto Me”. Every phrase of this has a history. The Gospel of John supplies much of the vocabulary, “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father”, “the Word was made flesh”; the Qur’an supplies the disclaimers, a mortal who eats food and walks in the markets, who does not know the unseen, whose hand was not his own when he threw; the Gītā and the prophets of Israel have their forms of the same claims. And every phrase has been contested. “God is not a man”, says the oracle; “my glory will I not give to another”; “say not Three”. Confucius denies that his knowledge was inborn, Shakespeare’s king is but a man, Emerson and Whitman claim for everyone what the readings reserve for a few, and Feuerbach turns the whole into a mirror of ourselves. The readings ask to be weighed in that company.
questions: “By what authority?” Compare the answer given in the readings with Jesus’ answer to John the Baptist and with the test in Deuteronomy. What kind of evidence does each accept, and what would Hume or Paine say to it?

The readings speak of a mirror in which God is seen and insist that the sun does not descend into it. How does this differ from “the Word was made flesh”, and does it meet the objections “God is not a man” and “say not Three”?

The knowledge of a Manifestation is said to be innate and complete. What do Luke’s “increased in wisdom”, Mark’s “neither the Son” and Confucius’s “I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge” ask of that claim?

The same voices say “I am but a servant” and “all turn unto Me”. How do the Qur’an’s disclaimers, the Gospel’s “why callest thou me good?” and “I and my Father are one” help in reading two such sentences together?
Can anyone reach the station of Christ? The readings say no; Emerson and Whitman say that everyone already stands there. What is at stake for ordinary people in each answer?
A crowd at Lystra took the apostles for gods, and an angel stopped John from kneeling. Where, in these readings, is the line between honouring a Messenger and what those passages forbid?

outside.why: The Manifestations are “heavenly Artists” who paint “with the brush of their deeds” in human hearts. The Qur’an says of its Prophet what makes such painting possible: in him there is a good example.
A clergyman asks: “By what authority is Bahá’u’lláh placed with Abraham, Moses and Jesus?” The chief priests put the same question to Jesus in the temple, in the same words.

The answer given to the clergyman points to teachings and their effect. When John the Baptist sent to ask “Art thou he that should come?”, the answer was of the same kind: report what you hear and see.

The reading tests a claim to prophethood by its teachings and their influence. Deuteronomy raises the question of a test outright and gives one: whether what the prophet says comes to pass. What can each test establish, and how long must one wait for it?

The Manifestation “must be the Educator, not the educated; His standard, intuition instead of tuition”. The crowd at the end of the Sermon on the Mount noticed that difference: he taught as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

A real Manifestation, the reading says, is “not dependent upon learning acquired in schools”. Confucius, the teacher of a whole civilization, said the opposite of himself: he was not born with knowledge, and sought it in antiquity. Is he then a different kind of teacher, or does the reading’s test exclude too much?

“There have appeared souls who became educators of humanity, who shone like the sun.” Carlyle built a theory of history on such figures, as great men, and put prophets among them beside poets and kings. What does the reading claim for them that “great man” does not say?
The Manifestations are “the true mirrors of the sanctified Essence of the Divinity”. The Letter to the Colossians uses a word of the same family for Christ: the image of the invisible God.
The reading quotes it: “He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father.” This is the exchange with Philip in which it is said.

The reading explains “God manifested in man” by a sun that does not descend into its mirror. The oracle of Balaam states the limit the explanation is guarding: God is not a man. Does the mirror keep that limit, and would the speaker of the oracle agree?

“Having barred the way that leadeth unto Thee”, God called into being the Manifestations of His Self. John’s prologue has the same two steps: no man has seen God at any time; the Son has declared Him.

Since the door of knowledge of the Hidden Essence is closed, the reading says, holy souls are sent. The Qur’an lists the only ways God speaks to a mortal: by revelation, from behind a veil, or through a messenger.
“The gates of knowledge and comprehension were closed.” The Tao Te Ching opens by closing the same gate: the Tâo that can be trodden, the name that can be named, are not the enduring ones.
“Prophets do not comprehend the God Essence.” In the Qur’an Jesus says so of himself to God: Thou knowest what is in my mind, and I know not what is in Thine.
The Prophets, the reading says, are exalted above the comprehension of men, “who can never know them except by their own Selves”. Jesus says that no one knows the Son but the Father.
“The Person of the Manifestation hath ever been the representative and mouthpiece of God.” The Qur’an says of Muḥammad that he does not speak of his own desire: it is an inspiration that is inspired.
The Manifestations occupy a material station, a human station and a station of divine manifestation. Tennyson addresses Christ across the same span: “Thou seemest human and divine”.

The reading gives the Manifestations a station above the human one. Shakespeare’s king, walking disguised among his soldiers, says what many have said of every exalted person: his ceremonies laid by, he is but a man. What would have to be shown to answer the soldier’s common sense?
The knowledge of the Manifestations, the reading says, “is divine and not acquired”. Luke says of the boy Jesus that he increased in wisdom. How do those who hold both read the word “increased”?

The universal Manifestations “are cognizant of all things”. Jesus says in Mark that of one day and hour neither the angels nor the Son knows, but the Father only. What kind of knowing does each sentence have in mind?
The station of a Prophet “is not acquired”; God chooses whom He will. Jeremiah is told that he was known and ordained before he was formed in the womb.
God has chosen the Prophets “from among His servants”. Amos, challenged by a priest, says how it was with him: no prophet, no prophet’s son, a herdsman taken from following the flock.

Can a person reach the station of Christ? The reading answers “No! It cannot be.” Emerson told a class of divinity students that Jesus saw what is true of everyone, and that he says to each hearer: see God in me, or in yourself when you think as I do. Which of them has understood the Gospels’ “I and my Father are one”?

The reading sets an uncrossable distance between Christ, who is “ancient”, and other people, who are “accidental”. Whitman announces his own divinity without waiting to be asked. What is lost, and what is protected, by the distance the reading keeps?
“All are from God but all have different stations.” The Qur’an says of the messengers that some were made to excel others, some were spoken to, and some raised in degree.

“The Blessed Perfection does not mean His body”, which lies in a tomb; the Reality is living. The Qur’an prepared the first Muslims for the same loss: Muḥammad is but a messenger; if he dies, will you turn back?

The Manifestations, the reading says, give up their personality so wholly that “their life is only the life of God”. The Qur’an says it of a single act at Badr: thou threwest not when thou didst throw, but God threw.
“I say not unto you that I know the unseen, nor do I claim any sign from heaven.” The Báb’s disclaimer follows, almost phrase for phrase, the one the Qur’an puts in Muḥammad’s mouth.
“He Who speaketh at the bidding of His Lord is but the First to worship Him.” Jesus turns aside even the title “good”: there is none good but one, that is, God.

There are kinds of Prophets, the reading says, some followers and promulgators, others universal. The Book of Numbers draws such a line: to a prophet God speaks in visions and dreams, but with Moses mouth to mouth.
“God has placed all the signs of the horizons within the souls.” The Báb is commenting on this verse of the Qur’an: signs on the horizons and within themselves, until the truth is manifest.

“None knows … your station for it is God’s station … nor your attributes for they are God’s attributes.” Isaiah’s God says that He will not give His glory to another. How is praise of this kind kept from being what Isaiah forbids?
“Were it not for you, nothing would know God; were it not for you, nothing would worship God.” The claim in John’s Gospel is the same in substance: no one comes to the Father but by me.

The reading makes all knowledge and worship of God depend on the Manifestations. The Buddha, dying, told his disciples to be lamps to themselves and to seek no refuge outside. What does a seeker owe to a teacher, and what must he do alone?
“The eyes of existence have never seen the like of Him.” Disciples have said as much of their masters in every tradition; Mencius reports it said of Confucius.

“If the Manifestations are subjected to tests, it is in Their human station only.” The Letter to the Hebrews values that human station for this very reason: a high priest tempted in all points as we are.
God created a reality that is “the channel of the supreme bounty … and the means of the highest gift”. The First Letter to Timothy calls Christ the one mediator between God and men.

The reading compares the few pages of Christ’s recorded words with the trunks filled by Bahá’u’lláh’s. John’s Gospel ends by saying that if everything Jesus did were written, the world could not hold the books. What is the worth of the comparison if most of one side was never written down?
The Manifestation is the embodiment of “He doeth whatsoever He willeth”. The Qur’an says of God that He is not questioned about what He does; others are.

The reading reserves to one being an essential infallibility and the right to do as He wills. Acton was writing about just such claims, made for popes and kings, when he said that power tends to corrupt, and absolute power absolutely. What distinguishes the reading’s claim from those he had in view?

“In Baghdad … He would go to coffeehouses and partake of coffee and the water pipe.” The objection behind that sentence is as old as the Qur’an: what kind of messenger eats food and walks in the markets?
“Do not think ill of your Lord.” Jesus was thought ill of on the same grounds: he came eating and drinking, and was called a glutton and a friend of sinners.
“They say the purpose of the Prophets … was to gain leadership and governance.” Pilate suspected it of Jesus and was told that the kingdom in question is not of this world.
“God is to every human being as great as the individual mental capacity permits one to see Him.” Xenophanes said it twenty-five centuries ago: oxen would draw their gods as oxen.

The reading allows that each person’s God is measured by that person’s mind. Feuerbach drew the conclusion the reading does not draw: that theology is anthropology, and the divine subject nothing other than the human. What does the reading hold that keeps it from his conclusion?
The reading heaps titles on the one who has come: the Hidden Secret, the Impenetrable Mystery. Isaiah gives the child who is to be born a like string of names.
The Tree of the Bayán, when grown, will be bent low “as a token of adoration” before the one who comes after. John the Baptist says of his own mission: he must increase, but I must decrease.

“The condemnation of God be upon him who regards me either as a representative of the Imam or the gate thereof.” Guru Gobind Singh warned his followers in the same tone against a title he would not bear.
The Báb curses those who give him a rank he rejects. The angel of the Apocalypse stops John from kneeling: I am thy fellowservant; worship God.

“Every Manifestation is but a revelation of Thine Own Self.” The chapter of the Qur’an that Muslims call Sincerity states God’s oneness against every such phrase: He begets not, nor was begotten, and none is comparable to Him. How does a faith born in Islam speak of “Thine Own Self” revealed and still say that chapter?
“Thy Manifestation in creation hath neither beginning nor end.” The voice in the Apocalypse calls itself Alpha and Omega, which is, and was, and is to come.
The reading speaks of Manifestation after Manifestation “from the days of Adam until now”. Krishna says that he comes whenever righteousness declines, from age to age.
“I have revealed the Books from God as He hath permitted Me, and have ordained ways as He hath willed.” Jesus says the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father do.
“All else was created for Him, for He is the mirror of Thy Self alone.” The Letter to the Colossians says of Christ that all things were created by him and for him.

“Verily I am the Mirror of God, my Lord; all turn unto Me.” The mystic al-Ḥallāj spoke of his union with God in words not unlike these, and was executed in Baghdad. What separates the claim of a Manifestation from the ecstasy of a mystic, in the eyes of those who hear either?

“All turn unto Me.” The first of the Ten Commandments allows no other gods before the one God, and no likeness of anything. How have traditions that keep this commandment made room for a human face turned toward?
“Whoso beholdeth Me with an eye besides Mine own will never be able to know Me.” Paul reasons that only the spirit of a man knows the things of a man, and only the Spirit of God the things of God.
“Barter not away this Youth … for the vanities of this world or the delights of heaven.” The merchant of the parable does the opposite trade: he sells all he has for one pearl.
The reading warns against bartering away the one who has come. The Gospel records the price for which that was once done.
“This is the Beauty of God amongst you … could ye but understand.” John’s prologue has the same sorrow: he was in the world, and the world knew him not.
“The Dawn hath appeared upon the Temple of Man. Verily this is the Book of the All-Merciful.” John says it in five words: the Word was made flesh.
Most people, “looking upon human habits manifested from the Divine Temple, remain veiled”. Nazareth is the Gospel’s example: is not this the carpenter, whose family we know?
The human form veils the one who appears in it. Krishna says the same of himself: the untaught mistake me, veiled in form.

The Essence, the reading says, is “sanctified above all limitations” and yet “hath appeared in human temple”. Xenophanes held the first half without the second: one god, in form and thought unlike mortals. What is gained by adding the human temple, and what does it risk?

“My station is but an image of Thy station … my very essence is but a reflection of the evidences of Thy unity.” The Letter to the Hebrews calls the Son the brightness of God’s glory and the express image of His person.
“He standeth in the place of God.” The phrase has a precedent in Exodus, where Moses is told: I have made thee a god to Pharaoh.
God “didst raise up from among Thy creatures One of Thy servants”, endued with signs. Isaiah’s servant is upheld and given the spirit, and his manner is described: he will not break a bruised reed.
“His love is Thy love, and His self Thy self.” In John, “I and my Father are one” is answered with stones, and the charge is stated: thou, being a man, makest thyself God.
“His Cause [is] Thy Cause.” The Qur’an says of those who gave their hands to Muḥammad that they swore allegiance to God: the Hand of God is above their hands.

“God testifieth that there is none other God but Him and that He Who hath appeared is the Hidden Mystery.” Israel’s confession stops after the first clause: the Lord our God is one Lord. What does the second clause add, and can it be added without taking from the first?
“Through Him His sovereignty, then His command, became manifest.” The risen Jesus says that all power is given to him in heaven and in earth.
“By God! He is this One, and this is the treasured Mystery.” Thomas, who had asked for proof, ends with a confession of five words.
“Whoso turneth unto Him hath in truth turned unto God … and whoso turneth away from Him hath turned away” from God. Jesus says it of himself and extends it to those he sends.
To turn to the Manifestation is to turn to God. The Qur’an: whoso obeys the messenger has obeyed God; and it adds that the messenger is no warder over those who turn away.
“The Most Great Sign, manifested in human form.” A confession quoted in the First Letter to Timothy begins: God was manifest in the flesh.

The reading speaks of the divine sign “in human form”. When a crowd at Lystra took Paul and Barnabas for gods in the likeness of men, the two tore their clothes and said they were men like any others. Where does reverence for a messenger become the error they ran to stop?
“He was hidden in the eternity of eternities, and when He willed to appear, He appeared.” John begins his Gospel before the appearing: in the beginning was the Word.
Moses longed for this presence, the reading says, and Muḥammad yearned for this countenance. Jesus tells his disciples that many prophets desired to see what they are seeing.

“Is it meet and seemly for you to question the authority” of such a one? Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor does more than question: he tells the returned Christ that nothing may be added to what was said of old, and that he has come to hinder the Church. Why would the guardians of a revelation be the last to welcome its author?
“If I be slain at your hands, God will assuredly raise up one who will fill the seat.” Gamaliel advised the council on that assumption: if it is of God, you cannot overthrow it.
The reading tells of a brother’s jealousy and a withdrawal to another house. John notes of Jesus, without comment, that his own brothers did not believe in him.
A decree ordered solitary confinement for life, and “His tent was raised” on the mountain all the same. Paul writes from his own chains that the word of God is not bound.
The strictest imprisonment did not hold. Lovelace wrote in prison that stone walls do not make one.
Was he subject to earthly rulers? Outwardly yes; “in reality He was not subject to any”. Jesus tells Pilate that the governor’s power over him is only what was given from above.
“Moses feared Pharaoh’s lack of belief, not fear for his life.” The Qur’an records the fear and its answer: we fear he may play the tyrant; fear not, I am with you both.
The dream of standing in the Imam’s place before a vast multitude has the shape of Joseph’s dream in the Qur’an, in which the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow.
“Through Thy face the face of the Desired One hath shone forth.” Paul speaks of the light of the knowledge of the glory of God “in the face of Jesus Christ”.

“Thou hast … made me to be the Day-Spring of Thy strength and the Manifestation of Thy might.” Shelley’s king also proclaimed his might to the mighty, and the sand has it now. What makes a claim to power the opposite of his?
The prayer asks that servants may “recognize Him Who is the Manifestation of Thy Self”. When Peter does recognize, he is told that flesh and blood did not reveal it to him.

The prayer asks for hearts cleansed so that they may recognize. Tennyson, in an age of proofs, says that this is embraced “by faith, and faith alone … believing where we cannot prove”. What part does evidence play in recognition, and what part something else?

“In prayer one must turn his face towards the Sanctified Reality of His holiness Bahá’u’lláh.” Asked which mountain was the right place of worship, Jesus answered that God is a Spirit and is worshipped in spirit and in truth. What does a direction give to prayer, and what does the answer to the Samaritan woman guard against?
The reading directs prayer toward a Reality that “surrounds all the phenomena”. Jesus says that whoever believes in him believes not in him but in the one who sent him.
The reading contrasts “the Joseph of Canaan” with the Joseph of the true Beauty. The Qur’an tells what the beauty of the first Joseph did to those who saw him: this is no human being.
The reading praises a “luminous countenance, divine comeliness, heavenly grace”. A royal psalm, long read of the Messiah, begins: thou art fairer than the children of men.

“Thy oneness is not established except through Him Who speaketh by Thy leave.” The Qur’an warned Christians that their language about Christ had endangered God’s oneness. How is oneness that is established “through” a person kept from that danger?

The Beloved unveiled himself “with a face like the shining moon and a beauty like the radiant sun”. Isaiah’s servant has no form or comeliness, “no beauty that we should desire him”. Is the beauty the reading sees one that every eye would see?
“Through His light He illumined the horizons.” Three disciples on a mountain once saw a face shine as the sun.
God raised him up, says the prayer, at one time with the name of Moses, at another with that of Jesus. John’s Gospel has a voice that speaks across the ages in the same way: before Abraham was, I am.
“Your Teacher and Instructor is Bahá’u’lláh.” The Gospel uses the fact of one teacher to level the taught: one is your Master, and all ye are brethren.
Through him “the law of oneness hath been revealed amidst the nations”, who turn toward one horizon. Daniel sees one like a son of man given a dominion that all peoples and languages shall serve.

leftOut.saying: “I know men, and I tell you that Jesus Christ is not a man.”
leftOut.attributed: Attributed to Napoleon on Saint Helena.
leftOut.reason: Wanted beside the readings that set a Manifestation apart from great men, and left out: it rests on reported conversation printed long afterwards and has no text of Napoleon’s to cut it from. Carlyle on great men stands there instead.

luke-he-that-heareth-you.text: He that heareth you heareth me; and he that despiseth you despiseth me; and he that despiseth me despiseth him that sent me

timothy-manifest-in-the-flesh.text: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory

acts-gods-come-down.text: And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men … Which when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of, they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people, crying out, And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you

john-brethren-did-not-believe.text: His brethren therefore said unto him, Depart hence, and go into Judaea, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest. For there is no man that doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, shew thyself to the world. For neither did his brethren believe in him

timothy-word-not-bound.text: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound

john-no-power-except.text: Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee? Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above

corinthians-face-of-jesus-christ.text: For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ

matthew-whom-say-ye.text: He saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am? And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven

john-in-spirit-and-in-truth.text: Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father … God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth

john-seeth-him-that-sent-me.text: Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me. And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me

psalm-fairer-than-the-children-of-men.text: Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever

isaiah-no-beauty.text: For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him

matthew-transfigured.text: And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light

matthew-one-is-your-master.text: But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren

daniel-son-of-man.text: I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed

quran-good-example.text: Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much.

quran-behind-a-veil.text: And it was not (vouchsafed) to any mortal that Allah should speak to him unless (it be) by revelation or from behind a veil, or (that) He sendeth a messenger to reveal what He will by His leave. Lo! He is Exalted, Wise.

quran-not-of-desire.text: Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire. It is naught save an inspiration that is inspired

quran-some-excel-others.text: Of those messengers, some of whom We have caused to excel others, and of whom there are some unto whom Allah spake, while some of them He exalted (above others) in degree

quran-but-a-messenger.text: Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him. Will it be that, when he dieth or is slain, ye will turn back on your heels

quran-allah-threw.text: And thou (Muhammad) threwest not when thou didst throw, but Allah threw

quran-treasures-of-allah.text: Say (O Muhammad, to the disbelievers): I say not unto you (that) I possess the treasures of Allah, nor that I have knowledge of the Unseen; and I say not unto you: Lo! I am an angel. I follow only that which is inspired in me

quran-horizons-and-themselves.text: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves until it will be manifest unto them that it is the Truth. Doth not thy Lord suffice, since He is Witness over all things?

quran-not-be-questioned.text: He will not be questioned as to that which He doeth, but they will be questioned.

quran-walketh-in-the-markets.text: And they say: What aileth this messenger (of Allah) that he eateth food and walketh in the markets? Why is not an angel sent down unto him, to be a warner with him.

quran-he-is-allah-the-one.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him

quran-swear-allegiance.text: Lo! those who swear allegiance unto thee (Muhammad), swear allegiance only unto Allah. The Hand of Allah is above their hands

quran-obeyeth-the-messenger.text: Whoso obeyeth the messenger hath obeyed Allah, and whoso turneth away: We have not sent thee as a warder over them.

quran-fear-not-i-am-with-you.text: They said: Our Lord! Lo! we fear that he may be beforehand with us or that he may play the tyrant. He said: Fear not. Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing

quran-gracious-angel.text: And when they saw him they exalted him and cut their hands, exclaiming: Allah Blameless! This is not a human being. This is no other than some gracious angel
quran-gracious-angel.caveat: Two slips in the page’s transcription of Pickthall (“no a human”, “not other”) are corrected.

analects-not-born-with-knowledge.text: I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there
analects-not-born-with-knowledge.author: Confucius

shakespeare-king-is-but-a-man.text: I think the king is but a man, as I am: the violet smells to him as it doth to me: the element shows to him as it doth to me; all his senses have but human conditions: his ceremonies laid by, in his nakedness he appears but a man
shakespeare-king-is-but-a-man.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

emerson-i-am-divine.text: One man was true to what is in you and me. He saw that God incarnates himself in man, and evermore goes forth anew to take possession of his world. He said, in this jubilee of sublime emotion, I am divine. Through me, God acts; through me, speaks. Would you see God, see me; or, see thee, when thou also thinkest as I now think
emerson-i-am-divine.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

whitman-divine-am-i.text: Divine am I inside and out, and I make holy whatever I touch or am touch'd from
whitman-divine-am-i.author: Walt Whitman

carlyle-biography-of-great-men.text: Universal History, the history of what man has accomplished in this world, is at bottom the History of the Great Men who have worked here
carlyle-biography-of-great-men.author: Thomas Carlyle
carlyle-biography-of-great-men.work: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History

mencius-never-another-confucius.text: Since there were living men until now, there never was another Confucius
mencius-never-another-confucius.author: Mencius

tennyson-strong-son-of-god.text: Strong Son of God, immortal Love, / Whom we, that have not seen thy face, / By faith, and faith alone, embrace, / Believing where we cannot prove
tennyson-strong-son-of-god.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-human-and-divine.text: Thou seemest human and divine, / The highest, holiest manhood, thou: / Our wills are ours, we know not how; / Our wills are ours, to make them thine
tennyson-human-and-divine.author: Alfred Tennyson

gita-veiled-in-form.text: The minds untaught mistake Me, veiled in form; — / Naught see they of My secret Presence, nought / Of My hid Nature, ruling all which lives
gita-veiled-in-form.locator: 9.11, in Edwin Arnold’s verse (The Song Celestial)

xenophanes-one-god.text: One god, the greatest among gods and men, neither in form like unto mortals nor in thought
xenophanes-one-god.author: Xenophanes

dostoevsky-come-to-hinder-us.text: I know too well what Thou wouldst say. And Thou hast no right to add anything to what Thou hadst said of old. Why, then, art Thou come to hinder us? For Thou hast come to hinder us, and Thou knowest that
dostoevsky-come-to-hinder-us.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

gobind-singh-gods-servant-only.text: All who call me the Supreme Being / Shall fall into the pit of hell. / Recognize me as God's servant only
gobind-singh-gods-servant-only.author: Guru Gobind Singh
gobind-singh-gods-servant-only.locator: in M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 5

hallaj-i-am-he-whom-i-love.text: I am He whom I love, and He whom I love is I: / We are two spirits dwelling in one body. / If thou seest me, thou seest Him, / And if thou seest Him, thou seest us both
hallaj-i-am-he-whom-i-love.author: al-Ḥallāj
hallaj-i-am-he-whom-i-love.work: verses, in R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam

feuerbach-theology-is-anthropology.text: the true sense of Theology is Anthropology, that there is no distinction between the predicates of the divine and human nature, and, consequently, no distinction between the divine and human subject
feuerbach-theology-is-anthropology.author: Ludwig Feuerbach
